fields.definition: In an oversampling (delta-sigma) analog-to-digital converter, the digital filter that low-pass filters the high-rate, coarsely quantized modulator output to remove out-of-band quantization noise and then reduces the sample rate (downsamples) to the target output rate, yielding full-resolution multi-bit PCM. By combining band-limiting with rate reduction it prevents aliasing on downsampling and largely sets the converter's passband flatness and stopband rejection.
fields.plain_english: A delta-sigma converter first runs at a very fast rate with rough numbers. This filter cleans out the extra noise and then slows the data down to the normal rate you use.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to turn the fast, noisy, low-resolution modulator output into clean, full-resolution audio at the wanted sample rate, rejecting energy above the new Nyquist frequency so downsampling does not cause aliasing.
fields.practical_application: A technician meets it as the fixed digital filtering inside an ADC, and on converters that offer filter choices it appears as selectable sharp or slow decimation responses that trade steepness against ringing.
common_mistakes: Confusing the decimation filter, which follows the modulator inside an ADC, with the reconstruction or anti-imaging filter that follows a DAC.
Assuming decimation just discards samples, when it must low-pass filter first or downsampling will alias noise back into the audio band.
Thinking the filter choice has no audible effect, when sharp and slow modes change pre-ringing and passband ripple.
scenario_contexts: Choosing a converter's sharp or slow filter mode for a mastering transfer.
Explaining why a 48 kHz ADC still runs its modulator at several megahertz internally.
Troubleshooting high-frequency roll-off traced to the decimation filter's passband edge.

sources: Analog Devices MT-022 and MT-023 tutorials, ADC/DAC architectures and sigma-delta conversion (manufacturer technical documentation)
Watkinson, The Art of Digital Audio (professional text)
Pohlmann, Principles of Digital Audio (professional text)

fields.definition: A converter (ADC or DAC) that uses a delta-sigma (sigma-delta) modulator to trade amplitude resolution for speed: it heavily oversamples the signal and drives a coarse, often one-bit or low-bit quantizer inside a feedback loop that noise-shapes the quantization error, pushing most of it above the audio band. A digital decimation filter (ADC) or an interpolation filter plus analog reconstruction filter (DAC) then removes that shaped noise, giving high effective resolution and dynamic range from simple, highly linear circuitry, which is why it dominates modern audio conversion.
fields.plain_english: This converter takes samples much faster than needed and uses rough steps. A feedback trick pushes most of the noise up high where a filter can throw it away, leaving clean audio.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to reach high resolution and dynamic range without needing extremely precise analog parts, using oversampling and noise shaping so the demanding work is handled in stable, low-cost digital filtering.
fields.practical_application: Nearly every audio interface, console, and outboard converter a technician uses today is delta-sigma, which is why these converters need a stable sample clock and why low-jitter clocking matters.
common_mistakes: Believing a one-bit modulator means only one bit of resolution, when noise shaping and decimation yield many effective bits.
Ignoring clock jitter, which directly degrades a delta-sigma converter's performance.
Confusing the internal oversampling ratio with the converter's output sample rate.
scenario_contexts: Adding an external low-jitter clock to get the best from an interface's delta-sigma converters.
Explaining to a student why a one-bit converter can still sound clean.
Comparing modern delta-sigma ADCs against older successive-approximation designs.

sources: Analog Devices MT-022 and MT-023 tutorials, sigma-delta ADC/DAC architectures (manufacturer technical documentation)
Watkinson, The Art of Digital Audio (professional text)
Pohlmann, Principles of Digital Audio (professional text)

fields.definition: A static converter error spec giving the deviation of each code step from its ideal one-LSB size, expressed in LSB. In an ADC, DNL more negative than -1 LSB produces missing codes; in a DAC, DNL of -1 LSB or worse makes the transfer function non-monotonic.
fields.plain_english: A converter should move in equal little steps. DNL measures how uneven those steps are. If one step shrinks too much, some values get skipped, like a ruler with a missing mark.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to quantify the evenness of individual code steps, warning of missing codes, added noise, and distortion caused by irregular step sizes.
fields.practical_application: A technician reads DNL in LSB on a converter datasheet to judge low-level linearity and sees its effects as extra noise or distortion on quiet passages.
common_mistakes: Confusing DNL, a step-to-step error, with INL, the overall bow of the transfer curve.
Assuming small DNL guarantees good INL, when many small step errors can accumulate into a large INL.
Thinking DNL has no audible effect, when large DNL raises the noise floor and adds distortion.
scenario_contexts: Comparing two converters' DNL specs when choosing an interface.
Explaining missing codes found during bench testing of a converter.
Relating measured low-level distortion back to a converter's DNL.

sources: Analog Devices MT-010 tutorial, ADC/DAC static specifications (manufacturer technical documentation)
IEEE Std 1241, Terminology and Test Methods for Analog-to-Digital Converters (standards body)
Pohlmann, Principles of Digital Audio (professional text)

fields.definition: The section of a signal chain that converts a stream of digital audio words back into a continuous analog voltage, typically an oversampling delta-sigma DAC built from a digital interpolation filter, a noise-shaped modulator, and an analog reconstruction (anti-imaging) filter, referenced to a sample clock. It is the boundary where digital data becomes analog audio at a given sample rate and bit depth, setting output level and noise floor and feeding downstream analog gain stages and outputs.
fields.plain_english: This is the part that turns digital audio numbers back into a real analog signal you can hear. It reads each value and builds a smooth voltage for your amps and speakers.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to convert stored or streamed digital audio into analog form for monitoring, mixing, and playback, defining the output level, noise floor, and analog interface to the rest of the system.
fields.practical_application: A technician feeds the DAC stage's line output into monitor controllers, amplifiers, or consoles and sets levels so the analog output stays below clipping in the following gear.
common_mistakes: Confusing the DAC stage, which is digital-to-analog at the output, with the ADC stage, which is analog-to-digital at the input.
Assuming more bits or a higher sample rate always improves the audible output, when analog stages and jitter often set the real limit.

UNSAFE: patching or power-cycling with DAC outputs unmuted and monitors live, since power-up and clock-loss transients can send full-scale thumps into amplifiers and speakers, risking hearing and equipment damage.
scenario_contexts: Connecting an interface's DAC output to powered monitors and setting a safe level.
Diagnosing distorted playback traced to a clipped DAC output stage.
Choosing a converter's reconstruction filter mode for critical monitoring.

sources: Analog Devices MT-017 tutorial, oversampling interpolating DACs (manufacturer technical documentation)
Watkinson, The Art of Digital Audio (professional text)
Pohlmann, Principles of Digital Audio (professional text)

fields.definition: A converter or audio-device spec stating, in dB, the ratio between the maximum full-scale signal level and the residual noise floor, defining the span between the loudest undistorted signal and the quietest resolvable one. Per the AES17 method it is measured with a low-level (typically -60 dBFS) signal present and referenced back to full scale, usually A-weighted, so it reflects usable range better than idle-channel noise alone.
fields.plain_english: This number tells you the gap between the loudest sound a converter can pass cleanly and the soft hiss underneath it. A bigger number means you hear quiet details without noise getting in the way.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to describe how much usable level range a converter has, helping technicians compare gear and set gain so both loud peaks and quiet detail survive.
fields.practical_application: A technician compares dynamic range figures (commonly about 110 to 123 dB A-weighted for good audio converters) when choosing interfaces and uses the concept to set gain staging that keeps signals well above the noise floor.
common_mistakes: Confusing dynamic range with signal-to-noise ratio, which uses different reference conditions even when the numbers look similar.
Assuming a 24-bit converter delivers its theoretical 144 dB, when analog noise limits real converters to roughly 120 dB.
Comparing dynamic range specs measured with different weightings, such as A-weighted versus unweighted, as if they were equal.
scenario_contexts: Comparing two interfaces' dynamic range specs before a purchase.
Explaining why a 24-bit converter does not deliver its theoretical 144 dB.
Setting gain staging so a quiet source stays above the converter's noise floor.

sources: AES17, AES standard method for measurement of digital audio equipment (standards body)
Analog Devices MT-003 tutorial, dynamic range and data-converter noise specs (manufacturer technical documentation)
Pohlmann, Principles of Digital Audio (professional text)

fields.definition: A figure of merit expressing a converter's real, measured resolution as an equivalent ideal bit count, derived from its measured signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio (SINAD) as ENOB = (SINAD in dB - 1.76) / 6.02. Because it folds in both noise and distortion, ENOB is always lower than the nominal nameplate bit depth.
fields.plain_english: A converter may say it is 24-bit, but noise and distortion waste some of those bits. ENOB tells you how many bits really carry clean audio, like counting only the ruler marks you can trust.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to give a single honest measure of real converter performance, letting technicians compare devices by usable resolution rather than by marketing bit counts.
fields.practical_application: A technician uses ENOB, often around 18 to 21 bits for good audio converters, to judge true performance and to understand why a 24-bit converter never delivers 24 clean bits.
common_mistakes: Treating nominal bit depth as if it were real resolution, ignoring that ENOB is always lower.
Computing ENOB from SNR alone, when the formula uses SINAD, which also includes distortion.
Comparing ENOB values taken at different input frequencies or amplitudes as if they were equivalent.
scenario_contexts: Reading a converter datasheet's ENOB to compare true resolution.
Explaining why 24-bit gear delivers around 20 effective bits.
Evaluating test-and-measurement digitizers by ENOB at a specified input frequency.

sources: IEEE Std 1241, Terminology and Test Methods for Analog-to-Digital Converters (standards body)
Tektronix, Understanding ENOB application note (manufacturer technical documentation)
Analog Devices MT-003 tutorial, converting SINAD to ENOB (manufacturer technical documentation)

fields.definition: A switch on a microphone or microphone preamp that inserts a high-pass (low-cut) filter into the signal path, attenuating frequencies below a set corner (commonly around 75 to 120 Hz) at a fixed slope (typically 6, 12, or 18 dB per octave) while passing higher frequencies. It reduces low-frequency rumble, handling and stage noise, wind, plosive energy, and the bass boost caused by proximity effect.
fields.plain_english: This switch cuts the deep low tones out of a mic signal. It helps remove rumble, thumps, and the extra boom you get when someone sings very close to the mic.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to remove unwanted low-frequency energy at the source, protecting headroom and reducing rumble and proximity buildup before the signal travels down the chain.
fields.practical_application: A technician switches the mic or preamp high-pass filter in for speech, vocals, and close-miked sources to tame rumble and plosives, and leaves it out for kick drum, bass, and other sources that need full low end.
common_mistakes: Setting the filter corner too high, thinning out vocals or instruments that need low end.
Engaging it on sources like kick and bass, weakening their fundamental.
Assuming a mic's built-in high-pass and a console's low-cut are identical, when their corner frequency and slope often differ.
scenario_contexts: Switching in a mic's low-cut for a lectern speech to reduce HVAC rumble.
Using the preamp high-pass on a close-miked vocal to control proximity boom and plosives.
Leaving the filter out when close-miking a kick drum for full low end.

sources: Neumann microphone technical data and operating manuals, low-cut filter specifications (manufacturer technical documentation)
Shure microphone technical data and application notes, low-frequency roll-off switches (manufacturer technical documentation)
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers (professional text)

fields.definition: A selectable converter operating mode that prioritizes conversion fidelity over power consumption or latency, typically by raising the oversampling ratio, using a sharper or more computationally intensive digital filter, and choosing lower-noise settings to maximize dynamic range and minimize distortion. It contrasts with low-power or low-latency modes that relax these parameters.
fields.plain_english: This is a setting that tells a converter to work its hardest for the best sound. It usually costs more power or a little more delay in trade for cleaner audio.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to let a device trade power use or latency for the best achievable audio quality when fidelity matters most, such as during critical recording or mastering.
fields.practical_application: A technician selects a high-quality or high-performance mode in an interface's control panel or a device menu when tracking or mixing, accepting slightly higher latency or power draw for better measured performance.
common_mistakes: Assuming the high-quality mode is always best, when its added latency can hurt live monitoring.
Thinking the mode name guarantees a specific spec, since implementations differ by manufacturer.
Leaving a battery-powered device in high-quality mode when low-power mode is needed for runtime.
scenario_contexts: Enabling a high-quality mode on an interface for a mastering transfer.
Choosing a low-latency mode instead during live overdub monitoring.
Comparing measured dynamic range between a converter's high-quality and low-power modes.

sources: Cirrus Logic audio codec data sheets describing high-performance and low-power converter modes (manufacturer technical documentation)
AKM audio converter data sheets describing selectable performance modes and digital filter options (manufacturer technical documentation)

fields.definition: A static converter error spec giving the maximum deviation of the actual transfer function from an ideal straight line, expressed in LSB or as a percentage of full scale, after gain and offset errors are removed. It is referenced to either an end-point line (through zero and full scale) or a best-fit straight line, and it equals the accumulated sum of the converter's DNL errors, so it predicts harmonic distortion.
fields.plain_english: A converter output should climb in a straight line as the input rises. INL measures how far the real line bends away from straight. A big bend means more distortion.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to quantify a converter's overall linearity, predicting the harmonic distortion caused by a curved rather than straight transfer characteristic.
fields.practical_application: A technician reads INL in LSB on a datasheet to gauge a converter's accuracy and distortion, keeping in mind that end-point and best-fit methods give different numbers.
common_mistakes: Confusing INL, the overall curve bow, with DNL, the step-to-step error.
Comparing INL specs without checking whether the end-point or best-fit method was used, since best-fit reads lower.
Ignoring that INL is specified after gain and offset errors have been removed.
scenario_contexts: Comparing converter datasheets' INL when accuracy matters.
Relating measured harmonic distortion back to a converter's INL.
Explaining why best-fit INL looks better than end-point INL on the same part.

sources: Analog Devices MT-010 tutorial, ADC/DAC static specifications (manufacturer technical documentation)
IEEE Std 1241, Terminology and Test Methods for Analog-to-Digital Converters (standards body)
Pohlmann, Principles of Digital Audio (professional text)
